statements.quote: For most of its history, AI was **symbolic**: explicit rules, logical inference, hand-curated knowledge.
The neural revolution displaced it, but did not destroy it.
The 2020s have seen a renaissance: knowledge graphs, formal verification, neuro-symbolic hybrids, and LLM agents that use tools and APIs as symbolic primitives.
This chapter traces the other branch of AI and shows how it complements neural networks.
Symbolic AI begins with the logicist dream that all of mathematics could be derived from logic.
statements.section: Before the program: logic and its limits

statements.quote: Frege's *Begriffsschrift* (1879) invented modern quantifier notation and tried to reduce arithmetic to logical laws; Russell and Whitehead's *Principia Mathematica* (1910-13) carried the project through, after Russell's paradox exposed its foundations (\cite[Frege, 1879]{frege1879}; \cite[Russell & Whitehead, 1910]{russell1910pm}; \cite[Russell's paradox]{russell_paradox_sep}).
statements.section: Before the program: logic and its limits

statements.quote: Hilbert's programme then asked for a finitary consistency proof and a decision procedure for first-order logic (\cite[Hilbert & Ackermann, 1928]{hilbert1928entscheidung}).
statements.section: Before the program: logic and its limits

statements.quote: Gödel's 1931 theorems ended the dream in its strong form: any consistent, effectively axiomatized system strong enough for arithmetic is incomplete and cannot prove its own consistency (\cite[Gödel, 1931]{godel1931incompleteness}; \cite[SEP]{sep_godel_incompleteness}).
statements.section: Before the program: logic and its limits

statements.quote: Turing's 1936 paper supplied the missing negative answer: no mechanical procedure can decide, for every first-order formula, whether it is provable (\cite[Turing, 1936]{turing1936}).
In 1950 he replaced the question of mechanism with an operational test -- can a machine's text replies be distinguished from a person's?
-- and made "Can machines think?" an empirical question (\cite[Turing, 1950]{turing1950computing}).

Six years later, the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project named the field and set its agenda: language, neural nets, abstraction, creativity, and the conjecture that every feature of intelligence can be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it (\cite[McCarthy et al., 1955]{mccarthy1955dartmouth}).
Before the technical material, it is worth pausing on the philosophical manifesto that grounded the entire symbolic-AI tradition in a defence of itself as a *science*.

statements.quote: Simon, in the ACM Turing Award lecture "Computer Science as Empirical Inquiry" (the 1975 award was given to Newell and Simon jointly, and the published paper is the joint form) — make a sustained case that computer science is not *applied mathematics* and not *engineering*, but an *empirical* science on a par with physics or biology, whose natural objects are **symbol systems** and whose characteristic method is the construction of *symbols and search*.

statements.quote: | | Symbolic (GOFAI) | Neural (Connectionist) |
| **Representation** | Symbols, rules, logic | Vectors, weights |
| **Reasoning** | Formal inference | Pattern recognition |
| **Knowledge** | Hand-curated | Learned from data |
| **Transparency** | Traceable proof | Black box |
| **Robustness** | Strong (provable) | Brittle (adversarial) |
| **Sample efficiency** | High | High data needs |
| **Scaling** | Knowledge engineering bottleneck | Compute + data |
Both have strengths the other lacks.
**Neuro-symbolic AI** is the synthesis.
The classical symbolic AI stack rests on **first-order logic** and its extensions.
statements.section: Knowledge Representation: From Logic to RDF

statements.quote: Variables are boolean; connectives $\land, \lor, \neg, \implies$ combine them.
Decidable; SAT solvers are highly optimized.
Adds $\forall$ (forall), $\exists$ (exists), predicates $P(x)$, and functions $f(x)$.
More expressive; semi-decidable.
A simple FOL knowledge base:
A fragment of FOL designed to be **decidable** while still expressive.
Foundation of the **Semantic Web**:
* **Concepts** (classes): Human, Mammal, Vehicle
* **Roles** (properties): hasParent, drives, owns
* **Individuals**: Socrates, Plato
* **Constructors**: $\sqcap$ (intersection), $\sqcup$ (union), $\neg$ (negation), $\exists R.C$ (exists role filler)
The standard **SROIQ** description logic underlies **OWL 2 DL** (the description-logic profile of the Web Ontology Language).
The Semantic Web stack (W3C standards):
* **RDF** (Resource Description Framework): triple representation $\langle \text{subject}, \text{predicate}, \text{object} \rangle$.
* **RDFS** (RDF Schema): class hierarchies, property hierarchies.
* **OWL** (Web Ontology Language): full description logic, cardinality constraints, equivalence, disjointness.
* **SPARQL**: SQL-like query language for RDF.
Major public knowledge graphs:
* **Wikidata**: 100M+ items, the open community-edited KG.
* **DBpedia**: extracted from Wikipedia infoboxes.
* **Google Knowledge Graph**: powers search infoboxes.
* **ConceptNet**: 34M commonsense assertions.
* **WordNet**: lexical KG (synonymy, hypernymy).
* **UMLS**: medical KG (3M+ concepts).
* **Amazon Product Graph, Facebook Entity Graph**: industrial-scale closed KGs.
A KG query is **graph pattern matching**:
Reasoners (Pellet, HermiT, FaCT++) implement **tableau-based** algorithms that check consistency and infer new triples.
* **Subsumption**: is $A$ a subclass of $B$?
* **Instance checking**: is $a$ an instance of $C$?
* **Consistency**: does the KG have a model?
* **Realization**: find the most specific class for an individual.
For **rule-based reasoning** beyond OWL, **Datalog** and **Prolog** are used.
Modern graph databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, Stardog, TigerGraph) add **property graphs**: nodes and edges with arbitrary attributes.
Resolution gave symbolic reasoning its industrial engine.

Robinson's 1965 rule -- resolve two clauses on a complementary literal, with unification handling variables -- made first-order theorem proving a single uniform inference step (\cite[Robinson, 1965]{robinson1965resolution}).

Kowalski's 1974 "Predicate Logic as a Programming Language" turned resolution into computation: a logic program is a set of Horn clauses, and answering a query is proof search (\cite[Kowalski, 1974]{kowalski1974prolog}).

Colmerauer and Roussel's Prolog (1972-73) implemented that idea and became the language of expert systems, natural-language parsers, and later Datalog engines (\cite[Colmerauer & Roussel, 1973]{colmerauer1973prolog}).
To bridge symbolic KGs with neural methods, several **KG embedding** methods learn vector representations of entities and relations:
* **TransE** \cite{bordes2013transe}: $\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} \approx \mathbf{t}$ (translation in embedding space).
* **DistMult** \cite{yang2015distmult}: bilinear $\langle \mathbf{h}, \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t} \rangle$ score.
* **ComplEx**: extends to complex-valued embeddings for asymmetric relations.
* **RotatE** \cite{sun2019rotate}: rotation in complex space, captures composition.
* **GraphSAGE** \cite{hamilton2017graphsage} / **R-GCN** \cite{schlichtkrull2018rgcn}: graph neural networks over the KG structure.
These enable **link prediction**: given $(h, r, ?)$, predict $t$, completing missing triples.
Used in recommendation, drug repurposing, fraud detection.
Symbolic AI's first commercial wave was knowledge engineering.

DENDRAL inferred molecular structures from mass spectra, MYCIN recommended antibiotics from hundreds of if-then rules, and both showed that hand-coded expertise could beat general search in a narrow domain (\cite[Feigenbaum et al., 1969]{feigenbaum1965dendral}; \cite[Shortliffe & Buchanan, 1976]{shortliffe1976mycin}).
The details explain why the recipe spread.

DENDRAL pruned the search for one compound from more than eleven million candidate structures to about twenty-two thousand, which could then be tested individually; MYCIN separated its rules from its inference engine, so the engine could be reused as the first expert-system shell (EMYCIN), and in a blind clinical test it prescribed antibiotics as well as, or better than, nine human clinicians \cite{crevier1993ai}.

The commercial breakthrough was XCON (originally R1), John McDermott's VAX configurer for the Digital Equipment Corporation: about three hundred rules in 1979 grew to more than three thousand by 1984, and the system configured ten machine models \cite{crevier1993ai}.
Winograd's SHRDLU (1972) embedded language in a tiny blocks world, so every word had a referent (\cite[Winograd, 1972]{winograd1972understanding}).
McCarthy and Hayes had already named the obstacle: the frame problem, deciding what stays unchanged when an action occurs (\cite[McCarthy & Hayes, 1969]{mccarthy1969some}).
Cyc, begun in 1984, was the maximalist response -- a hand-built common-sense ontology and inference engine -- but knowledge acquisition did not scale (\cite[Cyc]{cyc_wiki}).

The semantic web was the attempt to make that knowledge public and composable: RDF triples, OWL ontologies, and SPARQL queries, standardized by the W3C and promoted in Berners-Lee, Hendler, and Lassila's 2001 *Scientific American* article (\cite[Berners-Lee et al., 2001]{berners2001sw}).
Google's 2012 Knowledge Graph showed the industrial version -- a proprietary graph of entities and relations behind search answers (\cite[Singhal, 2012]{singhal2012knowledge}).

The current revival is neuro-symbolic: neural networks handle perception and ambiguity, while symbolic engines supply exact inference and verification, as in DeepProbLog and AlphaGeometry (\cite[Manhaeve et al., 2018]{manhaeve2018deepproblog}; \cite[Trinh et al., 2024]{trinh2024alphageometry}; \cite[Garcez & Lamb, 2020]{garcez2020neurosymbolic}).
Modern LLMs use **tools** as symbolic primitives:
* **Web search**: query → fetch results → summarize.
* **Code execution**: generate Python → run in sandbox → use output.
* **Calculator**: “what is 17 × 23?” → call a calculator → return 391.
* **Database query**: “users in Berlin” → generate SQL → execute → return rows.
* **API calls**: “book a flight” → call Skyscanner API.
Frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph, OpenAI's function-calling, Anthropic's tool use.
The LLM acts as a **planner and natural-language interface**; the symbolic system provides **grounded computation**.
Symbolic AI is critical for **provable correctness**:
* **Lean, Coq, Isabelle, Agda**: interactive theorem provers.
Used in mathematics (Liquid Tensor Experiment), cryptography (zk-SNARKs), and verified software (CompCert, seL4).
* **SAT solvers** (CaDiCaL, Kissat, CryptoMiniSat): scale to millions of variables.
Industry-standard for hardware verification, planning, scheduling.
* **SMT solvers** (Z3, CVC5): extend SAT with theories (arithmetic, arrays, bit-vectors).
* **Model checkers** (SPIN, TLC for TLA+): verify state machines, distributed systems, protocols.
The Lean-based **“AI for math”** initiative (DeepMind, 2024; OpenAI, 2024) has produced LLMs that:
Generate a candidate proof in natural language + Lean code.
Submit to Lean's kernel for verification.
If verification fails, refine using the error message.
The combined AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry system (\cite[DeepMind, 2024]{deepmind2024alphaproof}) reached silver-medal level at IMO 2024, solving four of the six problems.
Subsequent work has solved IMO 2025 problems.
The combination of **neural intuition** + **symbolic verification** is the most promising path to provably correct mathematical reasoning.
The synthesis takes several forms:
| Approach | Description | Example |
| **Neural + symbolic modules** | NN does perception, symbolic does reasoning | AlphaGeometry (\cite[Trinh et al., 2024]{trinh2024alphageometry}), AlphaProof |
| **Neural representations, symbolic inference** | Embeddings + logical rules | Logic Tensor Networks, NLProlog |
| **Symbolic priors on neural nets** | Constraints in loss function | Physics-informed NNs, constraint satisfaction |
| **NN as heuristic for symbolic search** | Learned policy for tree search | AlphaGo, theorem provers |
| **Differentiable logic** | Soft logic, gradient through rules | DeepProbLog, NARS |
| **LLM + tool use** | Neural planner, symbolic tools | ReAct \cite{yao2023react}, Toolformer, agents |
Solves IMO (\cite[Trinh et al., 2024]{trinh2024alphageometry}) problems: a Transformer generates candidate constructions, a symbolic DDAR (deductive database) verifies.
Solved 25 of the 30 IMO geometry problems from 2000–2022, close to the average human gold medallist.

A Transformer that learns to **call APIs** (calculator, search, translation) by self-supervised training on examples where API calls improve perplexity (\cite[Schick et al., 2023]{schick2023toolformer}).
Pure neural, but uses symbolic tools.
Embed logical rules as soft constraints on neural network outputs.
Combines first-order logic with deep learning in a single end-to-end trainable system.
Extends ProbLog (probabilistic logic programming) with neural predicates (\cite[Manhaeve et al., 2018]{manhaeve2018deepproblog}).
A neural net outputs probabilities; the probabilistic logic engine reasons over them.
* **Exact computation** (arithmetic, code execution)
* **Formal verification** (proofs, model checking)
* **Structured prediction with hard constraints** (valid JSON, valid SQL, valid chemical structures)
* **Deterministic reproducibility** (same input → same output)
* **Long-tail factual queries** (a KG knows every entity; an LLM hallucinates)
When you need provable, deterministic, exact results: use a symbolic system, possibly wrapped by an LLM as the interface.
* Open-ended generation (text, images, audio, video).
* Pattern recognition (vision, speech, anomalies).
* Tasks where rules are unknown or hard to specify.
* Handling natural-language inputs robustly.
By 2030, the standard production AI system will be:
* An LLM at the top, doing natural-language understanding and planning.
* Calling symbolic tools (calculators, code interpreters, databases, KGs, APIs).
* With formal verification of critical outputs.
* Trained jointly on text, code, and structured data (SQL, JSON, RDF).
The dichotomy is dissolving.
The student who masters **both** branches will be far more capable than one trained in either alone.
